keyVerseText: And every thing whereupon any part of their carcase falleth shall be unclean; whether it be oven, or ranges for pots, they shall be broken down: for they are unclean, and shall be unclean unto you.
rootMeaning: The root word כּוּר (kûwr) conveys the idea of a furnace or a pit that is dug or excavated, emphasizing a place of intense heat or transformation. The word כִּיר (kîyr) is etymologically connected to כּוּר and appears as a dual form, suggesting a structure designed to support two pots or vessels for cooking. This root sense enriches the common English gloss of 'stove' or 'cooking range' by highlighting the functional and physical nature of the object as a constructed site of heat, essential for preparation and transformation of food.
usageInScripture: The term כִּיר (kîyr) occurs only once in Scripture, specifically in Leviticus 11:35, where it is translated as 'ranges for pots' or simply 'ranges.' This singular occurrence shows a precise use related to a practical household or cultic context involving cooking or heating. The consistency in translation as a cooking apparatus underscores its role as a tangible, everyday object that also carries ritual implications in the purity laws of Israel.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כִּיר as a cooking furnace or range deepens our appreciation of the holiness code's concern with purity extending even to the tools and implements used in daily life. It reminds believers that God's call to holiness encompasses all spheres, including ordinary domestic activities. The cooking range, as a place where transformation occurs through heat, can metaphorically point to the refining work of God in the believer's life. This word, therefore, invites reflection on how physical objects and actions are not neutral but can be set apart or defiled, highlighting the comprehensive nature of God's sanctifying work through Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 11:35 states that anything on which the carcass of an unclean animal falls becomes unclean, including 'oven, or ranges for pots,' which must be broken down. The use of כִּיר here emphasizes that even the cooking ranges—intimate, everyday instruments—are subject to the holiness standards of Israel. This stresses the seriousness of God's purity laws and the extent to which defilement can permeate one's environment, calling for thorough cleansing and separation. The word thus enriches the verse by illustrating the tangible reality of maintaining holiness in all aspects of life.
